title: The gambit and its idea
intro:
The Vienna Gambit gives a pawn away on move three to open the f-file and take the centre: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4. The move order is the whole trick. The knight on c3 guards e4, which is exactly the square the f-pawn stops covering the moment it moves.

## What the pawn buys

Three things. The f-file opens for a rook that is already sitting on f1, so the attack needs no preparation. The pawn that lands on e5 becomes a wedge in front of Black's king, taking f6 and d6 away from his pieces. And d4 follows, so White finishes with pawns on d4 and e5 against a centre that has been cleared out.

The piece homes are short enough to remember: knights to c3 and f3, bishop to d3, pawn to d4, castle short, and the rook is already on the file it wants.

## Your second answer to 1...e5

You already play the Ruy Lopez Exchange against 1...e5, and this is the opposite question asked in the same position. The Exchange asks what a structure is worth in an endgame: trade on c6, keep the healthier majority, and grind. The Gambit asks what a pawn is worth for a file and a centre, and that question is answered by move fifteen or not at all. A second quiet system would only teach you a shape you already have.

## Where it is honest

Against the best reply, 3...d5, White is not better. The main lines of chapter 1 measure level, and a chapter promising more than that would be lying to you. What White gets is a position where every piece has a job and Black has to know what he is doing. Against everything else, from 3...exf4 to the third moves that decline, White is genuinely better, and often much better.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Playing f4 before Nc3, so that ...d5 hits e4 with nothing guarding it. Taking on e4 with a knight when the pawn on e5 is doing more work than a knight would. Starting the attack before d4 and castling are in. And treating every Black reply as if it were 3...d5: most of the others lose material to a plain recapture, and this course shows which.

tree.note: The first move of the repertoire. Everything here follows from the king's pawn and the knight that comes next.

children.note: The reply this course answers. Black takes his share of the centre and opens his own bishop.
The Vienna move, and the reason the gambit works at all. The knight guards e4 so that the f-pawn can leave it.

mistakes.note: The King's Gambit, which is a different opening and a much bigger one. Here it is out of order: after 2.f4 d5 the e4 pawn has nobody looking after it.
Perfectly good, and it is the move your Ruy Lopez plays. This course exists to ask the other question.

children.note: Black develops and hits e4. This is the main move and the one the course is built around.
The gambit. White offers the e-pawn a target and opens the f-file, trusting the knight on c3 to hold e4 for one more move.

mistakes.note: The quiet Vienna. Sound, and it teaches the same slow chess your Ruy already teaches, which is why it is not the course.
The other quiet Vienna, with the bishop going to g2. Also sound, also a different course.

children.note: The correct answer, and the only one that keeps Black level. Black hits back in the centre instead of taking the pawn.
Take. The pawn that lands on e5 is the wedge the whole system leans on, and it drives the f6 knight away from the centre.
Black grabs back rather than retreat. The knight on e4 looks strong and is really just short of squares.
Develop and hold e5. The modern main line: White finishes the setup instead of chasing the knight.

mistakes.note: This hands Black the centre back after 5...dxe4, and the pawn on e5 loses its support. Leave the knight alone and build.
The old main line, hitting e4 and d5 at once. Playable, and it costs more memorising than Nf3 does.

children.note: Black develops and prepares to castle, keeping the knight on e4 for now.
The other half of the centre. Pawns on d4 and e5 take every good square from Black's minor pieces.
Black tucks the king away before anything opens up.
The bishop aims at h7 and challenges the knight on e4 at the same time.
Black props the knight up with a pawn and stops Bxe4 being an option.
Take en passant. Leaving the pawn on e5 would let Black seal the position, and taking keeps the f-file open, which is what White paid for.

mistakes.note: Retreating lets Black play ...c5 and seal the centre. The f-file is the asset, so keep it open.

children.note: Black recaptures with the bishop, which keeps the knight on e4 and eyes d4.
Castle, and the rook lands on the open f-file without being moved.
Black brings the last minor piece out and adds a second attacker to d4.
Now the trade is right. Black's knight is the piece holding his position together, and taking it opens the long light diagonal for the bishop.

mistakes.note: The check loses a piece. 10...Nxc3 11.bxc3 dxc4 takes the bishop, because the knight on e4 was the only thing holding d5.

children.note: Black must take back with the pawn, which leaves that pawn loose on e4.
Collect it. White is level on material with the better minor pieces and the open file.
Black takes the d-pawn back at once rather than let White settle.
Develop with a hit on the knight. Everything White owns is now on a good square and the game is balanced.

mistakes.note: The pawn is not free. 12...Bxb7 takes the bishop straight back, and the knight on d4 still comes to f3 with check on top of it.

children.plan: Finish with c3 or Qd2 and double on the f-file. The bishop pair and the file are worth about what Black's activity is worth, so play for the small edge and do not force it.
